explanations.explanation: Egypt it is. Verse 3 says, “and they played in Egypt, prostituting themselves from their youth.” Verse 8 then says Oholah never gave up what she began there. Egypt is where the trouble starts in this picture.

Moab is a real land next to Israel, but the text never puts the sisters there. Verse 3 says, “and they played in Egypt…” and that is the place God names. Moab is a fine guess, but this one sends us back to Egypt.

Edom is another real neighbor of Israel, but this passage never mentions it. God points to Egypt: “and they played in Egypt, prostituting themselves from their youth.” That's the land where it all began for these two sisters.

Jerusalem is right. God says it plainly in verse 4: “Oholibah is Jerusalem.” Judah's kings reigned from there (1 Kings 14:21). So when God talks about the younger sister, He is talking about that city.

Shechem is a real city in Israel's story, but God doesn't name it here. Verse 4 says, “Oholah is Samaria, and Oholibah is Jerusalem.” The younger sister is Jerusalem. Shechem is a nice guess, but it isn't the city on this page.

Jericho is the city whose walls fell down (Joshua 6:20), so I understand why it came to mind. But God doesn't use it in this picture. Verse 4 says, “Oholibah is Jerusalem.” That's the city where Judah's kings reigned.

True. Verse 5 says, “Oholah prostituted herself while she was still Mine.” She already belonged to God and still went after other lovers. That is the heart of this whole picture, and it's a heavy one.
Verse 5 says the opposite: “Oholah prostituted herself while she was still Mine.” She belonged to God and still chased other lovers. That's what makes the picture so heavy.
The Assyrians, yes. Verse 5 says Oholah lusted after “her lovers, the Assyrians.” Verse 6 describes them as governors, commanders and horsemen. God names them straight out.
The Philistines are never mentioned in these verses. Verse 5 says Oholah lusted after “her lovers, the Assyrians.” Keep the name Assyria handy, because it comes back later in this chapter.
The Moabites don't appear in this part of the chapter. God says in verse 5 that her lovers are “the Assyrians.” Those are the warriors in blue, with the governors and commanders.
Idols is the word. Verse 7 says, “She defiled herself with all the idols of those for whom she lusted.” God ties the Assyrians to their idols. That's a big part of what is going on here.
Weapons make sense with warriors on horseback, but God doesn't say that. Verse 7 says, “She defiled herself with all the idols of those for whom she lusted.” Idols are what she took on, not weapons.
Treasures would be a reasonable guess, but verse 7 doesn't use the word. It says, “She defiled herself with all the idols of those for whom she lusted.” So the word is idols.

True. Verse 9 says, “Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted.” The ones she chased became the ones who ended up with her. It's a hard verse, and I won't pretend otherwise.
Verse 9 says, “Therefore I delivered her into the hands of her lovers, the Assyrians for whom she lusted.” So God did hand her over to the very lovers she chased. It's a hard line to read, friend.

That's not what verse 10 says. It says her lovers “seized her sons and daughters, and put her to the sword.” They took the children instead of protecting them. This is one of the heaviest lines in the chapter.
False is right. Verse 10 says her lovers “seized her sons and daughters, and put her to the sword.” They didn't protect anyone. It's a heavy verse, so take a breath here, friend.

Yes. Verse 11 says Oholibah saw what happened to Oholah, “yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.” She saw all of it, and it didn't turn her around. That's the sobering part.

explanations.answer: She turns back to God for good
explanations.explanation: I wish the verse went that way, friend. Verse 11 says she saw what happened to her sister, “yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.” She saw it and kept going. So no turning back here.

explanations.answer: She grieves and stays away from lovers
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say she grieved or stayed away. Verse 11 says she saw it, “yet in her lust and prostitution she was more depraved than her sister.” She went further down the same road.
True. Verse 12 says, “She too lusted after the Assyrians.” The details match too: governors, commanders and horsemen. Verse 13 sums it up: “both of them had taken the same path.”
Verse 12 says, “She too lusted after the Assyrians.” They're the same governors, commanders and horsemen her sister chased. Verse 13 says it outright: “both of them had taken the same path.”

Babylonians is right. Verse 15 says the men on the wall “looked like officers of the Babylonians in Chaldea, the land of their birth.” She saw them engraved on a wall in vermilion. Chaldea is the land the Babylonians come from.
The Egyptians do show up in this chapter, but not on this wall. Verse 15 says the men looked like “officers of the Babylonians in Chaldea.” Egypt comes in later, when her mind goes back to her youth.
The Persians are never mentioned in this passage. Verse 15 says the men looked like “officers of the Babylonians in Chaldea, the land of their birth.” So the wall pictures Babylonians.
Messengers, yes. Verse 16 says she “sent messengers to them in Chaldea.” She saw pictures on a wall and sent word across the distance.
Gifts is a fair guess, but the verse doesn't say that. Verse 16 says she “sent messengers to them in Chaldea.” The word is messengers.
The text never says she sent soldiers. Verse 16 says she “sent messengers to them in Chaldea.” Messengers carry words, and soldiers carry swords.
That's right. Verse 17 says that after the Babylonians defiled her, “she turned away in disgust.” Keep that line in mind, because it comes back in the next stop.
The text doesn't say she begged them to stay. Verse 17 says, “But after she had been defiled by them, she turned away in disgust.” She is the one who turned away.

explanations.answer: She wants to marry their king
explanations.explanation: A royal wedding would be quite a plot twist, but the verse never goes there. Verse 17 says, “But after she had been defiled by them, she turned away in disgust.” Disgust is the word.
True. In verse 18 God says, “I turned away from her in disgust, just as I had turned away from her sister.” Both sisters ended up in the same place with Him.
Verse 18 says, “I turned away from her in disgust, just as I had turned away from her sister.” So God treated Oholibah the same way as Oholah. It was the same turning away.
It would be nice if memory worked that way. Verse 19 says, “Yet she multiplied her promiscuity, remembering the days of her youth.” Looking back made her go further, not turn around.
False is right. Verse 19 says, “Yet she multiplied her promiscuity, remembering the days of her youth.” Looking back didn't turn her around. It made things worse.
Verse 22 says otherwise. God says, “I will bring them against you from every side.” Not one side, every side. There's no corner left to hide in.
False is right. In verse 22 God says, “I will bring them against you from every side.” That means all around her, not one direction.

Their own standards, yes. Verse 24 says, “I will delegate judgment to them, and they will punish you according to their own standards.” God hands the judgment over, and they carry it out by their own measure.
The law of Moses isn't mentioned in these verses. Verse 24 says, “they will punish you according to their own standards.” Their standards, not Israel's.
The text doesn't point to Jerusalem's laws. Verse 24 says, “I will delegate judgment to them, and they will punish you according to their own standards.” The enemy's standards are the ones in play.
True. Verse 25 says, “They will seize your sons and daughters.” Verse 10 says the same thing happened to Oholah. The sisters share this heavy fate.
Verse 25 says, “They will seize your sons and daughters.” That matches what verse 10 says about Oholah. Both sisters share this hard outcome.

Right. Verse 27 says, “So I will put an end to your indecency and prostitution, which began in the land of Egypt.” It began in Egypt and God says it ends here. She will not “lift your eyes to them or remember Egypt anymore.”
Verse 27 doesn't say that. God says, “So I will put an end to your indecency and prostitution, which began in the land of Egypt.” What ends is the behavior, not her name.
A line of kings isn't mentioned in this verse. Verse 27 says, “So I will put an end to your indecency and prostitution, which began in the land of Egypt.” That's the thing God says He will end.

explanations.answer: Chasing the nations and their idols
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 30 says, “because you have prostituted yourself with the nations and defiled yourself with their idols.” God spells out the reason Himself, so we don't have to guess.
Curses from prophets aren't in the text. Verse 30 gives the reason: “because you have prostituted yourself with the nations and defiled yourself with their idols.” God names the cause plainly.

explanations.answer: A famine sent on her fields
explanations.explanation: Verse 30 doesn't mention a famine. It says these things came “because you have prostituted yourself with the nations and defiled yourself with their idols.” The reason is the nations and their idols.
That's it. Verse 31 says, “Because you have followed the path of your sister, I will put her cup into your hand.” Same path, same cup. God gives the reason in the same sentence.
The text never says she mocked her sister. Verse 31 gives the reason: “Because you have followed the path of your sister, I will put her cup into your hand.” She followed her sister's path.

explanations.answer: She took over her sister's land
explanations.explanation: Taking over land isn't mentioned here. Verse 31 says, “Because you have followed the path of your sister, I will put her cup into your hand.” The reason is the path she followed.
True. Verse 34 says, “You will drink it and drain it.” The cup is deep and wide, and she will drain it to the bottom. It's a heavy word, friend.
Verse 34 says, “You will drink it and drain it.” So the cup is not left half full. It's a heavy word, and God means every bit of it.

explanations.answer: She forgot Him and pushed Him aside
explanations.explanation: Yes. Verse 35 says, “Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back, you must bear the consequences of your indecency and prostitution.” God puts it in His own words.

explanations.answer: She feared her enemies more than Him
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say that. Verse 35 says, “Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back…” Her fear of the enemy isn't mentioned.

explanations.answer: She never heard His word spoken
explanations.explanation: That isn't what the verse says. God says, “Because you have forgotten Me and have cast Me behind your back, you must bear the consequences of your indecency and prostitution.” Forgetting and casting aside are the reasons given.
